lessons.title: Edward Bernays — Core concepts
concepts: Edward Bernays (1891-1995), Freud's nephew, founded modern public relations as an applied social science: Crystallizing Public Opinion (1923) defined the 'public relations counsel,' and Propaganda (1928) openly argued that shaping public attitudes is the necessary work of democratic leadership — before 'propaganda' became a slur.

The core techniques: third-party authority (borrow credibility from trusted groups), manufactured events (stage news the press must cover, as in the 1929 Torches of Freedom parade), and framing (define the terms of debate so your conclusion feels inevitable). Each works by managing context, not by arguing facts.

'The Engineering of Consent' (1947) extended PR from products to governance: democratic leaders, Bernays claimed, must deliberately mold public opinion. The democratic objection is that consent engineered through concealed interests is managed, not given.

Astroturfing and front groups are the industrial descendants: a paid interest rents a citizen identity to borrow grassroots credibility. The tell is always provenance — who funds the messenger — and the remedy is disclosure.

Media literacy is the defensive discipline: ask who paid for the message, who the cited authorities really are, what was staged versus what happened, and how the issue is framed. Every Bernays technique has a corresponding audit question.

The persuasion/manipulation line is operational, not aesthetic: persuasion survives disclosure and preserves the audience's ability to dissent; manipulation requires concealment and bypasses rational agency. Run every campaign through the publicity test.

example.code: printf '%s\n' "CLAIM: Doctors recommend Brand X" "CHECK: who funded the study?" "CHECK: are the doctors real, independent, representative?" "CHECK: what did the study actually measure?" "CHECK: who profits if I believe this?" > literacy-checklist.txt && cat literacy-checklist.txt
example.walkthrough: A media-literacy checklist is a procedure, not a vibe: provenance, independence, evidence, incentive. Running any claim through these four checks is the practical application of everything Bernays teaches in reverse.

pitfalls: Common trap: calling everything 'propaganda' — Bernays used the word neutrally in the 1920s for organized persuasion; the useful distinction now is persuasion versus manipulation, not PR versus 'truth.'
Common trap: assuming media literacy means cynicism — the goal is calibrated trust (knowing which claims survive audit), not believing nothing.
Common trap: focusing on the message while ignoring the messenger — Bernays' whole method is that credibility is borrowed; audit the lender.
Common trap: thinking disclosure kills persuasion — honest campaigns with disclosed interests (public health, safety) persuade openly; only manipulation needs the dark.
lessons.try_it: Work through this in the Labs tab.

concepts: Time-box your sessions: 50 minutes of focused work, 10 minutes off. Three focused sessions beat one exhausted six-hour grind.
Active recall beats re-reading: after each lesson, close it and explain the key idea out loud in your own words before moving on.
The strategic communication exam rewards pattern recognition. Every scenario you answer builds a mental library of 'I've seen this shape before.'
Track your weak domains explicitly. Revisit them with the systems-anatomy lens: trace the full flow, find where your mental model breaks.

example.code:
WEEKLY RHYTHM (example)
  Mon/Wed/Fri: 2 new domains (lessons + labs)
  Tue/Thu: scenario drills on prior domains
  Sat: timed mock assessment
  Sun: review misses, rebuild weak areas
example.walkthrough: Elite performers don't study more hours — they study with tighter feedback loops. Every wrong answer is a precise map of what to fix next.

pitfalls: Passive highlighting and re-reading — feels productive, builds nothing.
Avoiding timed practice until 'ready' — the clock is a skill, train it early.
Studying only strengths — comfort is the enemy of growth.
lessons.try_it: Write down your three weakest areas right now. You will re-test them at the end of this bootcamp.

lessons.title: Bernays & Public Relations: Field Overview
concepts: The big picture first: Bernays & Public Relations sits at the intersection of theory you must know and judgment you must demonstrate.
Employers and examiners test the same thing: can you reason from first principles when the situation is novel, not just recite facts?
Every domain in this bootcamp maps to a real capability: something you will actually do, decide, or explain on the job.
The capstone at the end proves you can integrate everything — that is the artifact you show, not just talk about.

example.code:
MAP OF THE TERRITORY
  Foundations → Core systems → Applied judgment → Capstone proof
  Each layer assumes the last. There are no shortcuts, only compounding.
example.walkthrough: Keep this map in mind as you work through domains. When a lesson feels abstract, ask: 'what real decision does this prepare me for?'

pitfalls: Treating domains as isolated trivia — they connect. Always ask how this domain touches the others.
Ignoring the 'why' behind procedures — procedures change, principles don't.
Waiting until the end to attempt the capstone — start scoping it now.
lessons.try_it: Skim the domain list for this bootcamp. Write one sentence for each: what real-world capability does it build?

lessons.title: How Assessment Works Here
concepts: Knowledge checks verify understanding before a lesson counts as complete — you prove it, then it counts. No click-through completions.
Scenarios are scored on judgment: the right answer with the right reasoning. Read every 'why' explanation even when you answer correctly.
The mock assessment is timed and cumulative. It draws on all domains — treat it as the real exam rehearsal.
Labs verify hands-on skill in the terminal. If a check fails, the hint tells you exactly what to fix — iterate until green.

example.code:
SCORING MODEL
  Lessons: completion requires passing the knowledge check
  Scenarios: attempts tracked, streaks build mastery
  Labs: all checks must pass
  Mock: scored like the real thing — this is your readiness signal
example.walkthrough: The system is designed so that 'complete' means 'can actually do it.' Respect the bar and it will carry you through the real assessment.

pitfalls: Gaming the knowledge check by guessing — it exists to protect you from false confidence.
Skipping lab hints — they are targeted coaching, not cheating.
Taking the mock once — take it repeatedly until your score stabilizes above target.
lessons.try_it: Answer this lesson's knowledge check, then run one terminal lab to feel the verification loop.

lessons.title: Capstone: Influence Campaign Analysis — Blueprint
concepts: Your capstone proves integrated capability: Analyze a real historical or contemporary influence campaign end-to-end: techniques used, channels, audience segmentation, and measurable outcomes — presented as a professional briefing.
Scope it in milestones, not monoliths. Each milestone is independently demonstrable — if you run out of time, you still have working pieces.
Document as you build. The artifact plus the write-up is what you show; either alone is half the value.
Build in public where appropriate: version control, clear commits, a README that explains the why, not just the what.

example.code:
CAPSTONE MILESTONES
  1. Select a campaign and gather primary sources (ads, speeches, coverage)
  2. Map every observed technique to the propaganda taxonomy
  3. Trace the audience segmentation and channel strategy
  4. Assess outcomes against stated objectives with evidence
  5. Deliver a 10-minute briefing with visual technique map
example.walkthrough: A capstone is graded on integration and judgment, not just completion. At each milestone ask: 'what decision did I make here, and why this way?'

pitfalls: Scope creep — freezing the milestone list on day one protects you.
Building without documenting — you will forget your own reasoning within days.
Perfectionism on milestone 1 — get all milestones to 'working' before polishing any to 'great.'
lessons.try_it: Write your milestone list now, with a definition of done for each.

lessons.title: Capstone: Build Log & Documentation
concepts: Keep a build log: date, what you attempted, what worked, what failed, what you learned. This becomes your documentation draft.
Your README needs five sections: what it is, why it matters, how to run it, architecture decisions, and what you'd do with more time.
Screenshots and terminal transcripts beat prose for proving hands-on work. Capture evidence as you go.
Anticipate the three hardest questions about your capstone and write the answers before anyone asks.

example.code:
README SKELETON
  # Title — one-line value proposition
  ## Why — the problem this solves
  ## Quickstart — commands to run it
  ## Architecture — decisions and trade-offs
  ## Next steps — honest limitations
example.walkthrough: Documentation written after the fact reads like fiction. The build log keeps it honest — and honesty about limitations reads as seniority.

pitfalls: README as an afterthought — start it on day one, even as stubs.
Hiding limitations — naming them with a plan reads as maturity.
No reproduction steps — if they can't run it, it doesn't exist.
lessons.try_it: Create your capstone repo/directory and write the README skeleton today.

lessons.title: Capstone: Demo & Defense
concepts: Prepare a 5-minute demo: the problem, your approach, the working result, one hard decision you made. Rehearse it out loud twice.
Defense prep: for every tool and choice in your capstone, be ready to answer 'why this instead of the alternative?'
Connect each capstone decision back to bootcamp domains — this shows integrated understanding, not isolated effort.
End your demo with honest next steps. 'Here's what I'd harden for production' is the strongest closing line.

example.code:
DEMO ARC (5 min)
  0:00 — The problem (30s)
  0:30 — Your approach (60s)
  1:30 — Live working demo (120s)
  3:30 — One hard decision + trade-off (45s)
  4:15 — Next steps for production (45s)
example.walkthrough: The demo is a performance. Rehearsal is what makes it look effortless — and effortlessness reads as mastery.

pitfalls: Demoing without a fallback — have screenshots/video if live fails.
Over-running time — a tight 5 minutes beats a rambling 15.
Memorizing a script — know the beats, speak naturally.
lessons.try_it: Do a timed 5-minute dry run of your demo this week, even if the build isn't finished.

lessons.title: The Seven Classical Devices
concepts: Name-calling: attaching negative labels to discredit without engaging the argument — 'radical,' 'corrupt' — works by triggering disgust before analysis begins.
Glittering generality: vague virtuous words — 'freedom,' 'progress' — that invite the audience to project their own meaning onto the message.
Transfer: borrowing authority by associating the message with respected symbols — flags, uniforms, religious imagery — so their prestige rubs off.
Testimonial: a admired figure endorses the message; the audience's trust in the person transfers to the claim without scrutiny.
Plain folks: the communicator poses as ordinary — rolled sleeves, diner visits — to dissolve the distance between elite sender and mass audience.
Card stacking: selective presentation of facts — true statements arranged to mislead by omission; the most defensible form of deception.
Bandwagon: 'everyone is doing it' — exploits social proof so the audience follows rather than evaluates.

example.code:
DEVICE SPOTTING DRILL
  Headline: 'Real patriots support the bill.'
  → Name-calling (implied: opponents aren't patriots)
  → Glittering generality ('real patriots')
  → Bandwagon ('support' as consensus)
  Three devices in five words. Train this reflex.
example.walkthrough: Devices rarely appear alone — professional messages layer 2-4. Your job is to decompose the stack, not just name one.

pitfalls: Calling everything propaganda — the devices are neutral tools; analysis requires identifying intent and truth-value too.
Missing card stacking — it's the hardest to spot because every individual claim can be true.
Confusing transfer with testimonial — transfer borrows symbols, testimonial borrows people.
lessons.try_it: Take today's front-page headline. List every device you can identify, with the exact words that trigger each.

lessons.title: Bernays and the Engineering of Consent
concepts: Bernays' core thesis: in a democracy, public opinion must be shaped deliberately by an 'invisible government' of PR professionals — he argued this was necessary, not sinister.
'Crystallizing Public Opinion' (1923): PR as applied social science — the counsel on public relations studies group psychology then designs stimuli.
The Torches of Freedom (1929): Bernays reframed cigarettes as feminist liberation symbols, doubling the market — the canonical case of engineering consent through third-party authority.
Method: he didn't advertise products; he engineered events and enlisted credible third parties (doctors, civic groups) so the message arrived as news, not ads.

example.code:
TORCHES OF FREEDOM — ANATOMY
  Objective: expand cigarette market to women
  Barrier: social taboo against women smoking
  Reframe: smoking = feminist emancipation ('torches of freedom')
  Vehicle: 1929 Easter parade, debutantes lighting up
  Authority: staged as news event, not advertisement
  Result: taboo broken, market doubled
example.walkthrough: Study Bernays for method, not morality. The exam tests whether you can dissect the mechanism: objective → barrier → reframe → third-party vehicle.

pitfalls: Reducing Bernays to 'he manipulated people' — the exam wants the mechanism, step by step.
Confusing PR with advertising — Bernays' innovation was earning media through engineered events.
Forgetting the third-party principle — the message must arrive from a trusted source, not the sponsor.
lessons.try_it: Pick a modern product launch. Identify the third-party validators enlisted and the reframe used.

lessons.title: Framing: The Battle Over Meaning
concepts: Framing selects which aspects of reality to emphasize — the same facts framed as 'estate tax' vs 'death tax' produce opposite coalitions.
Equivalence framing: logically identical options get different responses based on presentation — '90% success' vs '10% failure' is the classic demonstration.
Issue framing determines who decides: framing healthcare as 'economic' vs 'moral' routes it to different committees, experts, and publics.
Reframing is the master skill: when you can't win inside the opponent's frame, change the frame — shift the question being answered.

example.code:
FRAME AUDIT
  'Tax relief' — frame: taxes are an affliction; relief is deserved
  'Revenue enhancement' — frame: taxes fund civilization; enhancement is responsible
  Same policy. Different moral universe. The frame does the arguing before arguments begin.
example.walkthrough: On the exam, when asked about messaging strategy, start with frame analysis: what frame is each side using, and which frame has structural advantage?

pitfalls: Debating inside a losing frame — if the frame implies your defeat, no argument wins.
Treating frames as spin — frames are cognitive infrastructure, not decoration.
Missing the meta-frame — who gets to define what the issue 'is about' usually wins.
lessons.try_it: Take a current policy debate. Write the two competing frames in one sentence each, then name the structural winner and why.

lessons.title: The Propaganda Model: Manufacturing Consent
concepts: Herman and Chomsky's model: five filters — ownership, advertising, sourcing, flak, ideology — that systematically shape news without conspiracy.
Ownership filter: concentrated corporate ownership sets boundaries of acceptable debate; journalists internalize limits as professionalism.
Sourcing filter: reliance on official sources makes the powerful the default definers of reality — 'according to officials' is a structural bias.
The model predicts coverage patterns: worthy vs unworthy victims — identical suffering gets opposite coverage based on alignment with elite interests.

example.code:
APPLYING THE FILTERS
  Story: foreign policy crisis
  1. Who owns the outlet? → what interests bound the frame?
  2. Who advertises? → what topics are soft-pedaled?
  3. Who are the sources? → officials vs victims ratio?
  4. Flak risk? → what can't be said without punishment?
  5. Ideology? → which -ism organizes the narrative?
example.walkthrough: You don't need to endorse the model wholesale — the exam tests whether you can apply the filters analytically to coverage patterns.

pitfalls: Treating the model as conspiracy theory — it's structural analysis, not accusation.
Applying filters selectively to outlets you dislike — the model claims universality.
Confusing flak with censorship — flak is post-publication punishment that disciplines future coverage.
lessons.try_it: Pick one major story. Run it through all five filters and write a 5-line audit.

lessons.title: What Public Opinion Is (and Isn't)
concepts: Public opinion is not a thing to be found but a process to be understood — polls capture a snapshot of a moving, often incoherent aggregate.
The attentive public vs the mass public: most people hold thin, unstable opinions on most issues; a small attentive stratum holds structured ones.
Non-attitudes: a large share of poll responses are pseudo-opinions manufactured on the spot — question wording creates the opinion it measures.
Opinion leadership: the two-step flow — media reaches opinion leaders, who interpret it for their circles. Persuade the leaders, move the followers.

example.code:
READING A POLL
  Topline: 54% support
  Ask: Who was sampled? What was the exact question?
  What preceded it? (order effects)
  Margin of error ±4 → real range 50-58
  'Support' of what, exactly? (non-attitude risk)
  A number without these answers is decoration.
example.walkthrough: Every poll you cite in analysis must survive these questions. The exam rewards poll literacy over poll quotation.

pitfalls: Treating polls as public opinion itself — they're instruments with error, not thermometers of truth.
Ignoring the attentive/mass distinction — strategies differ completely by stratum.
Missing non-attitudes — citing thin opinions as mandates.
lessons.try_it: Find a recent poll. Write the five-question audit: sample, wording, order, error, meaning.

lessons.title: Opinion Formation and Change
concepts: Priming: media doesn't tell people what to think, but what to think about — agenda-setting moves the salience, not the position.
Framing effects on opinion: the same policy gets majority support or opposition depending on which considerations are primed.
Socialization agents: family, school, peers, media — early formation is sticky; conversion is rare, mobilization is the realistic goal.
The spiral of silence: people suppress views they believe are minority, which makes majority views look bigger — polls can manufacture the consensus they report.

example.code:
PRIMING CHAIN
  Week 1: heavy crime coverage (agenda: crime salient)
  Week 2: candidate talks 'tough on crime' (primed audience receptive)
  Week 3: polls show crime top concern (manufactured salience read as demand)
  The coverage created the concern it then 'responded' to.
example.walkthrough: For strategy questions, think in sequences: what gets primed first determines what arguments land later.

pitfalls: Confusing agenda-setting with persuasion — salience vs position are different levers.
Assuming opinions are stable traits — most are constructed in the moment of asking.
Forgetting the spiral — visible consensus may be enforced silence.
lessons.try_it: Map a priming chain for a current issue: what coverage preceded the current 'public concern'?

lessons.title: Polling Methodology Essentials
concepts: Sampling: probability samples let you generalize; opt-in online panels don't — the method determines what the number means.
Question wording effects routinely swing 10-20 points: 'welfare' vs 'assistance to the poor' measures different things.
Likely-voter screens are models, not observations — two pollsters' LV models can produce different leaders from identical data.
Weighting corrects known skews but bakes in assumptions; unweighted raw data is not more honest, just differently wrong.

example.code:
POLL AUTOPSY
  Claim: 'Candidate leads by 6'
  Sample: 800 LV, MoE ±3.5 → lead is inside noise
  Wording: 'If election were held today...' (hypothetical)
  Dates: conducted during opponent's scandal week (event effect)
  Verdict: noise + timing, not a lead.
example.walkthrough: Never cite a poll without the autopsy. On the exam, the poll-literate answer beats the poll-quoting answer.

pitfalls: Treating MoE as the only error — systematic error (bad sample, bad model) dwarfs sampling error.
Horse-race tunnel vision — issue and favorability internals matter more than the topline.
Ignoring timing — polls are events, not trends; one poll is weather, aggregates are climate.
lessons.try_it: Autopsy one poll from this week's news using the four-question method.

lessons.title: The Two-Step Flow and Opinion Leaders
concepts: Katz and Lazarsfeld: media effects flow through opinion leaders — people are more influenced by trusted peers than by broadcasts.
Opinion leaders are not elites: they're the most engaged members of each social circle — the friend everyone asks about cars, health, politics.
Modern version: micro-influencers and community nodes outperform mass reach for persuasion; virality is leader-to-follower cascades.
Strategy implication: map the leader network first. A message with no leader carriers dies; with carriers, it multiplies.

example.code:
LEADER MAPPING
  Issue: vaccine uptake in a neighborhood
  Broadcast: citywide ad (reach high, persuasion low)
  Two-step: brief 12 trusted community figures (reach low, persuasion high)
  Result: leader-carried message outperforms broadcast 3:1 on behavior
  Persuasion travels through trust, not bandwidth.
example.walkthrough: When a scenario asks about campaign design, start with: who are the opinion leaders for this audience, and what carries the message to them?

pitfalls: Targeting 'the public' as an undifferentiated mass — persuasion is always networked.
Confusing reach with influence — impressions don't move people, trusted voices do.
Ignoring leader incentives — leaders carry messages that serve their standing.
lessons.try_it: For your community: name three opinion leaders on one issue and what would motivate each to carry a message.

lessons.title: Agenda-Setting: What to Think About
concepts: McCombs and Shaw: media doesn't tell people what to think, but what to think about — issue salience follows coverage volume.
First-level agenda-setting transfers issue salience; second-level transfers attribute salience — which aspects of the issue matter.
Need for orientation: agenda-setting effects are strongest when the issue is relevant but unfamiliar — high relevance plus high uncertainty.
Policy agenda interaction: media, public, and policy agendas influence each other — coverage can force issues onto the legislative calendar.

example.code:
AGENDA TRACE
  Month 1: 12 stories on transit delays (salience rising)
  Month 2: polls show transit top-3 concern (public agenda moved)
  Month 3: council announces transit task force (policy agenda moved)
  Coverage → salience → pressure → action. The chain is the theory.
example.walkthrough: Use agenda-setting to explain why some issues explode and others, equally serious, never register.

pitfalls: Claiming media tells people what to think — that's the rejected hypodermic model.
Ignoring second-level — attributes matter as much as issues.
Forgetting reverse flow — policymakers also set media agendas.
lessons.try_it: Trace one current issue through the three agendas: media, public, policy. Where's the lead?

lessons.title: Uses and Gratifications: The Active Audience
concepts: The audience is not a passive target — people select media to gratify needs: information, identity, entertainment, social connection.
Implication for strategists: messages compete with everything else serving those needs. 'Important' loses to 'gratifying' unless you fuse them.
Selective exposure: people choose congenial content — persuasion must cross the selection barrier before it can work.
The active audience reinterprets: the same message produces oppositional, negotiated, or dominant readings (Hall's encoding/decoding).

example.code:
GRATIFICATION AUDIT
  Message: policy explainer video
  Competing gratifications: entertainment (cat videos), identity (tribe content), social (group chat)
  Design fix: embed the explainer inside entertainment + identity payoffs
  If it doesn't gratify, it doesn't get watched.
example.walkthrough: Design every message for the audience's needs, not your objectives. Their gratifications are the toll road your message must travel.

pitfalls: Assuming attention is free — it's the scarcest resource; earn it with gratification.
One reading per message — plan for oppositional and negotiated decodings.
Ignoring selective exposure — your message must survive the choice to engage.
lessons.try_it: Audit your last message: which gratification did it serve for the audience? Be honest.

lessons.title: Cultivation: The Slow Drip
concepts: Gerbner: heavy media consumption cultivates a worldview — mean-world syndrome from crime-heavy diets is the canonical finding.
Effects are slow and cumulative, not from single messages — cultivation is about the steady-state diet, not the viral moment.
Mainstreaming: heavy viewers across groups converge toward a shared outlook — differences narrow under a common media diet.
Strategic use: long campaigns shift baselines; don't expect single ads to cultivate — plan the drip over months.

example.code:
CULTIVATION MATH
  Heavy viewer: 4+ hrs/day crime content
  Perceived risk of victimization: 3x actual rate
  Voting: 'tough on crime' +25 vs light viewers
  No single show caused it — the diet did.
example.walkthrough: When a scenario involves long-term attitude shifts, reach for cultivation: what diet, over what time, produces what baseline?

pitfalls: Expecting quick cultivation wins — the theory is explicitly long-horizon.
Confusing with agenda-setting — salience (weeks) vs worldview (years).
Ignoring mainstreaming — the convergence prediction is testable and distinctive.
lessons.try_it: Estimate a heavy-viewer diet in your issue area. What baseline would it cultivate over a year?

lessons.title: The Attention Economy
concepts: Attention is the scarce resource; content is abundant — the competition is not other messages on your issue, but everything competing for the same eyeballs.
Algorithmic amplification rewards engagement, and outrage engages — the system structurally favors polarizing content regardless of anyone's intent.
Agenda-cutting: the flip side of agenda-setting — keeping issues off the agenda through flooding, distraction, or algorithmic suppression.
Strategy: design for the algorithm's incentives (early engagement, watch time) while serving your substantive goals — the package must win the feed first.

example.code:
FEED SURVIVAL
  Your explainer vs: outrage clip, cute animal, friend's baby
  Algorithm scores: predicted engagement in first 60 seconds
  Design: hook in 3 seconds, payoff pattern every 20s, share trigger at end
  Substance rides inside the engagement vehicle.
example.walkthrough: Every distribution plan must answer: why does the algorithm show this to anyone? 'It's important' is not an answer the feed accepts.

pitfalls: Planning distribution as an afterthought — the feed decides reach before merit does.
Chasing virality over strategy — viral and persuasive are different goals.
Ignoring agenda-cutting — sometimes the fight is about what never trends.
lessons.try_it: Write the 3-second hook for your most important message. Test it on one person today.

lessons.title: Cialdini's Six Principles
concepts: Reciprocity: people repay what they receive — even unsolicited favors create obligation pressure. Free samples aren't generosity; they're leverage.
Commitment/consistency: once people take a small public step, they align future behavior to stay consistent — the foot-in-the-door sequence.
Social proof: in uncertainty, people follow the herd — testimonials, crowd counts, and 'most popular' labels manufacture certainty.
Authority: titles, uniforms, and credentials trigger automatic deference — the Milgram lesson applied to marketing.
Liking: we say yes to people we like — similarity, compliments, and cooperation manufacture liking on purpose.
Scarcity: restricted availability inflates value — deadlines and limited stock convert deliberation into urgency.

example.code:
PRINCIPLE STACK (fundraising email)
  'As a valued supporter [liking]...'
  '...join 48,000 donors [social proof]...'
  '...before midnight tonight [scarcity].'
  'P.S. Here's our impact report [reciprocity].'
  Four principles, one email. Professionals stack them.
example.walkthrough: Memorize the six as a diagnostic checklist: for any persuasive message, name which principles fire and how.

pitfalls: Using principles manipulatively without regard for truth — persuasion without substance is fraud with better branding.
Forgetting the boundary conditions — scarcity fails when the offer is unwanted; authority fails when distrusted.
Applying principles to yourself uncritically — the checklist also defends you.
lessons.try_it: Take one ad you saw today. Tag every Cialdini principle present with the exact triggering words.

lessons.title: Cognitive Biases in Persuasion
concepts: Anchoring: the first number frames all that follow — 'was $500, now $200' makes $200 feel cheap regardless of true value.
Loss aversion: losses hurt ~2x more than gains please — 'don't lose your coverage' beats 'gain peace of mind.'
Confirmation bias: people accept congenial claims uncritically and scrutinize uncongenial ones — preach to the convertible, not the choir or the hostile.
Availability heuristic: vivid examples outweigh statistics — one story beats a thousand data points in persuasion (though not in truth).

example.code:
BIAS LEVERAGE MAP
  Price presentation → anchoring (show premium first)
  Call to action → loss aversion (what they lose by waiting)
  Audience targeting → confirmation (persuadables, not partisans)
  Proof format → availability (one vivid case + data appendix)
example.walkthrough: Ethical line: biases are facts about cognition. Using them to help people choose well is persuasion; using them to mislead is manipulation.

pitfalls: Leading with statistics against vivid stories — you'll lose; pair data with narrative.
Targeting the unconvertible — confirmation bias makes hostile audiences immune.
Ignoring your own biases — the analyst is also a cognitive miser.
lessons.try_it: Rewrite one of your messages using all four biases deliberately. Note where each fires.

lessons.title: Elaboration Likelihood: Two Routes
concepts: Central route: high elaboration — the audience thinks carefully; argument quality decides. Works when motivation and ability are high.
Peripheral route: low elaboration — cues decide: source attractiveness, message length, emotional tone. Works when motivation or ability is low.
Match the route to the audience: experts get central-route arguments; mass audiences get peripheral cues wrapped around a simple core claim.
Sleeper effect: over time, people forget the discredited source but retain the message — peripheral wins can outlast their dubious origins.

example.code:
ROUTE MATCHING
  Policy experts → central: data, mechanisms, trade-offs (they'll scrutinize)
  General public → peripheral: trusted messenger, vivid story, simple ask
  Mixed audience → layered: peripheral hook opens, central substance for those who engage deeper
example.walkthrough: The most common failure: central-route arguments delivered to peripheral-route audiences — brilliant briefs nobody processes.

pitfalls: Assuming everyone processes centrally — elaboration is the exception, not the rule.
Pure peripheral with no substance — wins attention, collapses under scrutiny.
Forgetting the sleeper effect — discount discredited sources' lingering influence.
lessons.try_it: Classify your last three messages by route. Did the route match the audience's elaboration likelihood?

lessons.title: Resistance and Inoculation
concepts: Persuasion triggers resistance: forewarning ('you're about to hear a pitch') inoculates by activating defenses before the message lands.
Inoculation theory: exposing people to weakened counterarguments builds resistance — like a vaccine, small doses of opposition strengthen the position.
Reactance: threats to freedom ('you must') trigger defiance — preserve autonomy ('the choice is yours') to keep the door open.
Stealing thunder: revealing your own weakness first defuses attacks — the opponent's ammunition is spent before they fire.

example.code:
INOCULATION SCRIPT
  'Some will say this costs too much. They're right that it requires investment —
   here's what that investment buys, line by line...'
  Weakened objection + refutation = immunized audience.
  When opponents later raise cost, the audience has already processed it.
example.walkthrough: Play defense as deliberately as offense: inoculate your audiences before opponents strike.

pitfalls: Surprising your own side with bad news — steal thunder early, always.
Triggering reactance with commands — 'consider' beats 'you must.'
Inoculating with strawmen — weakened versions must be fair or the vaccine fails under real attack.
lessons.try_it: Write an inoculation paragraph for your position's strongest objection. Keep it honest.

lessons.title: Campaign Architecture
concepts: Every campaign has five load-bearing walls: objective (measurable), audience (segmented), message (framed), channels (mapped to audience), and timeline (sequenced). Remove one and it collapses.
Objectives must be behavioral, not attitudinal: 'raise turnout 4 points in Ward 7' beats 'raise awareness' — awareness is not a strategy.
Segmentation before messaging: persuadables, base (mobilize), opponents (ignore or inoculate against). One message for all three fails all three.
The calendar is a weapon: work backward from decision day, sequencing priming → persuasion → mobilization → GOTV. Each phase has different metrics.

example.code:
CAMPAIGN SKELETON
  Objective: +4 turnout, Ward 7, Nov 5
  Segments: base 30% (mobilize), persuadable 25% (persuade), opposed 45% (ignore)
  Message: base='stakes', persuadable='values+proof', opposed=inoculate base
  Channels: base=SMS+volunteers, persuadable=local news+leaders
  Timeline: priming (wk1-4) → persuasion (wk5-8) → mobilization (wk9-10)
example.walkthrough: If you can't fill all five walls for a campaign, you don't have a campaign — you have activities hoping to become one.

pitfalls: Attitudinal objectives — 'awareness' without behavior is theater.
Unsegmented messaging — the average message persuades no one.
Front-loading everything — sequencing matters more than volume.
lessons.try_it: Draft the five walls for a hypothetical campaign in one page.

lessons.title: Message Discipline
concepts: One campaign, one message, repeated relentlessly: 'It's the economy, stupid' — discipline beats creativity in campaigns.
The message triangle: three supporting points, all laddering to the core message. Every surrogate, ad, and speech stays inside the triangle.
Bridging: answer the question you were asked, then bridge to your message — 'that's important, and what voters really need to know is...'
Rapid response: the 24-hour rule is dead; it's now the 24-minute rule. Pre-drafted responses for predictable attacks, war-room for the rest.

example.code:
MESSAGE TRIANGLE (example)
  Core: 'Safer streets through community policing'
  Point 1: Officers who know the neighborhood
  Point 2: Response times cut in half
  Point 3: Youth programs that prevent crime
  Every interview, ad, and speech: pick a point, land the core.
example.walkthrough: Discipline is the multiplier: a mediocre message repeated beats a brilliant message mentioned once.

pitfalls: Message of the day syndrome — novelty for the staff bores the voters who just heard it first.
Answering hostile frames directly — bridge, don't debate on their turf.
Slow response — unanswered attacks become true by repetition.
lessons.try_it: Write your core message in 8 words, then build the triangle beneath it.

lessons.title: Paid, Earned, Shared, Owned
concepts: PESO model: Paid (ads you buy), Earned (coverage you earn), Shared (social amplification), Owned (channels you control: email, SMS, site).
Earned is the most credible and least controllable; paid is the most controllable and least credible. Great campaigns convert paid into earned.
Owned is the only durable asset — algorithms change, but your list is yours. Build the list with every paid and earned touch.
Shared is the multiplier: design messages with share triggers (identity, emotion, utility) so audiences distribute for you.

example.code:
PESO MIX (ballot measure)
  Paid 40%: persuasion ads to persuadables
  Earned 25%: event stunts + data drops for coverage
  Shared 15%: volunteer toolkit, shareable graphics
  Owned 20%: list-building ads → email/SMS for GOTV
  Every dollar tracked to a behavioral objective.
example.walkthrough: Audit any campaign by PESO: which quadrant is missing? That's usually why it's failing.

pitfalls: 100% paid — renting attention with nothing owned at the end.
Ignoring shared — no share triggers, no multiplication.
Confusing earned with deserved — coverage must be engineered, not hoped for.
lessons.try_it: Map your last effort across PESO. Which quadrant was starved?

lessons.title: Metrics That Matter
concepts: Vanity metrics (impressions, likes) measure activity; decision metrics (persuasion shift, turnout, conversion) measure outcomes. Report the latter.
Tracking polls measure movement, not position — the trend line matters more than any single number; watch the slope.
A/B testing: test message variants on small segments before scaling — 10% test, 90% scale beats 100% guess.
The one metric: cost per behavioral outcome (per vote, per donor, per conversion). Everything else is diagnostic.

example.code:
DASHBOARD THAT MATTERS
  North star: cost per vote ($/behavioral outcome)
  Movement: tracking poll slope (not level)
  Funnel: reach → engagement → persuasion → action (leakage per stage)
  Tests: variant A vs B, n, lift, decision
  Vanity (impressions) goes in the appendix.
example.walkthrough: If your dashboard can't answer 'what do we do differently Monday?', it's decoration.

pitfalls: Optimizing vanity metrics — cheap impressions that move nobody.
Single-poll panic — trends over points, always.
No test discipline — opinions about messages are cheap; tests are truth.
lessons.try_it: Define the north-star behavioral metric for your effort and the current cost per unit.

lessons.title: The Golden Hour
concepts: In a crisis, the first hour sets the narrative frame — silence is filled by others, and the first frame is the stickiest.
Speed vs accuracy trade-off: say what you know, say what you're doing, say when you'll update — 'we don't know yet' beats silence.
The holding statement buys time without lying: acknowledge, express concern, state action, promise updates. Never speculate.
Internal first: employees hear it from you before the press, or they become the press's sources.

example.code:
HOLDING STATEMENT TEMPLATE
  'We are aware of [incident]. Our immediate priority is [safety/people].
   We have [action taken]. We will update at [time] with verified facts.
   We will not speculate until [investigation] is complete.'
  60 words. Buys hours. Commits to nothing false.
example.walkthrough: Prepare holding statements before you need them. The golden hour has no time for drafting from scratch.

pitfalls: 'No comment' — reads as guilt and cedes the frame entirely.
Speculating to fill airtime — one wrong fact destroys all future credibility.
Forgetting internal audiences — your people are your first public.
lessons.try_it: Draft a holding statement for your organization's most plausible crisis. Time yourself: under 15 minutes.

lessons.title: Apology Mechanics
concepts: Effective apologies have four parts: acknowledge specifically, accept responsibility, explain corrective action, make amends. Missing any part fails.
The non-apology apology ('mistakes were made,' 'if anyone was offended') inflames — passive voice and conditional offense deny the injury.
Timing: too fast looks glib, too slow looks forced. The window is after facts are known but before the narrative hardens — usually 24-72 hours.
The spokesperson must match the gravity: the CEO apologizes for institutional failures; delegating reads as evasion.

example.code:
APOLOGY AUTOPSY
  Bad: 'We regret if any inconvenience occurred.' (conditional, vague, passive)
  Good: 'We exposed your data. I approved the system that failed. Here's the fix, here's your protection, here's my direct line.'
  Specificity + ownership + action + access = credibility.
example.walkthrough: Write apologies you'd respect receiving. The test is always: would the injured party feel heard?

pitfalls: The conditional 'if' — 'if anyone was offended' apologizes for their feelings, not your act.
Blaming systems without human ownership — 'processes failed' needs a name attached.
Apologizing for the reaction instead of the act — 'sorry you're upset' is gasoline.
lessons.try_it: Rewrite a famous non-apology into a real one using the four-part structure.

lessons.title: Stakeholder Triage
concepts: In crisis, rank stakeholders by impact and influence: victims first, then regulators, employees, partners, media, public — in that order.
Each stakeholder needs a different message: victims need care and remedy; regulators need compliance facts; employees need clarity and protection.
The media is never the first audience — it's the channel to the real audiences. Brief victims before cameras.
Map stakeholder information needs hourly in the first day; stale stakeholders become hostile stakeholders.

example.code:
TRIAGE MATRIX
  Victims: care + remedy + direct line (hourly)
  Regulators: facts + cooperation (as required)
  Employees: what happened + their role + job safety (before press)
  Media: verified facts only (scheduled updates)
  Public: values + action (after victims briefed)
example.walkthrough: Triage prevents the classic failure: performing for cameras while victims learn from Twitter.

pitfalls: Media-first instinct — cameras are loud but victims decide the verdict.
One message for all — regulators and victims need different truths emphasized.
Set-and-forget — stakeholder needs evolve hourly; re-triage continuously.
lessons.try_it: List your top five crisis stakeholders in order, with each one's first-hour information need.

lessons.title: Recovery and Reputation Rebuild
concepts: Recovery has three phases: stabilize (stop the bleeding), reform (fix the cause visibly), rebuild (earn trust through sustained action).
Reform must be visible and structural — firing one person reads as scapegoating; changing the system reads as learning.
Third-party validation accelerates rebuild: auditors, watchdogs, and reformed critics carry more credibility than self-praise.
The timeline is 3-5x longer than leaders expect — reputation rebuilds at the speed of demonstrated change, not announcements.

example.code:
RECOVERY ARC
  Days 1-7: stabilize — contain, care, communicate
  Weeks 2-8: reform — independent review, structural changes, published
  Months 3-12: rebuild — sustained action, third-party audits, quiet consistency
  Announce less, demonstrate more. Trust compounds slowly.
example.walkthrough: Plan recovery before the crisis: the reform playbook written calmly beats the one improvised under fire.

pitfalls: Declaring victory early — 'we've learned our lessons' before demonstrating change.
Cosmetic reform — new slogans without structural change get exposed.
Impatience — rushing the timeline reads as insincerity.
lessons.try_it: Sketch the 12-month recovery arc for your most plausible crisis scenario.

lessons.title: Reading Like an Analyst
concepts: Separate the layers: facts (verifiable), framing (emphasis choices), and persuasion (devices) — most confusion comes from mixing them.
Source triangulation: one outlet is a claim; three independent outlets are evidence. Independence matters more than count.
Follow the incentives: who profits if you believe this? The cui bono question clarifies more than fact-checking alone.
Timestamp discipline: old stories recirculate as new — check dates before reacting; outrage at expired news is manufactured engagement.

example.code:
ANALYST READ PROTOCOL
  1. Facts: what is verifiably claimed? (highlight)
  2. Sources: named? independent? primary?
  3. Frame: what aspects emphasized/omitted?
  4. Devices: which persuasion techniques fire?
  5. Incentives: cui bono if believed?
  6. Date: current or recirculated?
example.walkthrough: Run this protocol on everything important before forming a view. Speed is the enemy of accuracy.

pitfalls: Single-source certainty — one report is a lead, not a conclusion.
Skipping incentives — the most clarifying question asked last.
Reacting to undated content — recirculation is a feature of manipulation.
lessons.try_it: Apply the six-step protocol to the top story in your feed right now.

lessons.title: Misinformation vs Disinformation
concepts: Misinformation is false but spread without intent to deceive — error. Disinformation is false and spread deliberately — weapon.
Malinformation: true information weaponized — real facts, selectively deployed to harm. The hardest category because fact-checks pass it.
Detection signals: emotional targeting (outrage/fear), false authority, manufactured consensus, and timing tied to decision points.
Response differs by type: misinformation gets correction; disinformation gets exposure of the operation; malinformation gets context restoration.

example.code:
TYPE → RESPONSE
  Misinformation (error) → correct gently, preserve relationship
  Disinformation (weapon) → expose the network, don't debate the claim
  Malinformation (weaponized truth) → restore the missing context
  Wrong response type wastes effort or backfires.
example.walkthrough: Diagnose the type before responding. Debating a disinformation claim legitimizes it; correcting it as error misses the operation.

pitfalls: Treating all falsehood as lies — error needs grace, weapons need exposure.
Fact-checking malinformation — the facts are true; it's the selection that's the attack.
Amplifying by debunking — repeating the claim spreads it; lead with the truth.
lessons.try_it: Classify three dubious items you saw this week: mis-, dis-, or malinformation?

lessons.title: Algorithmic Literacy
concepts: Your feed is not the world — it's a prediction of what keeps you engaged, built from your past behavior. Everyone's 'reality' differs.
Engagement optimization favors the emotional and the tribal — the algorithm doesn't hate truth; it's indifferent to it.
Filter bubbles are partly self-built: every click trains the next feed. Your diet is your curation, whether intentional or not.
Counter-measures: follow primary sources, seek disconfirming voices deliberately, use chronological feeds where available, take information fasts.

example.code:
FEED AUDIT
  Scroll 20 items. Tally: agrees with me / challenges me / neutral.
  If challenges < 3, your feed is a mirror, not a window.
  Fix: add 5 primary sources + 3 thoughtful disagree-ers.
  Re-audit monthly. Curation is maintenance.
example.walkthrough: You can't think clearly on a diet engineered for engagement. Curate like your judgment depends on it — it does.

pitfalls: Assuming the feed is representative — it's representative of your clicks.
Outrage as information — anger is engagement fuel, not evidence.
Passive consumption — the algorithm curates you unless you curate it.
lessons.try_it: Do the 20-item feed audit today. Write down the tally.

lessons.title: Evaluating Expertise
concepts: Credentials signal training, not correctness — ask: relevant expertise? track record? conflicts of interest?
Consensus matters: one expert vs the field's consensus — mavericks exist but the base rate favors consensus on settled questions.
Distinguish experts from communicators: the best explainer isn't always the best researcher — value both, confuse neither.
Prediction track records: for forecasters, score past predictions. Pundits with no scoreboard are entertainers.

example.code:
EXPERT SCORECARD
  1. Relevant domain expertise? (not just fame)
  2. Consensus position or outlier? (base rates)
  3. Conflicts/funding? (cui bono)
  4. Track record on predictions? (scoreboard)
  5. Uncertainty acknowledged? (honest experts hedge)
  3+ green: trust provisionally. 2+ red: discount heavily.
example.walkthrough: Apply the scorecard before amplifying any expert claim. Virality is not peer review.

pitfalls: Credential worship — titles without relevant track records.
Maverick romanticism — outliers are sometimes right and usually wrong.
Ignoring conflicts — funding shapes findings more than fraud does.
lessons.try_it: Scorecard one expert you cited recently. Report the tally honestly.

lessons.title: Ethics Frameworks for Persuasion
concepts: Deontology: some tactics are wrong regardless of outcome — lying, astroturfing, and manufactured consensus violate duties to truth.
Consequentialism: judge by outcomes — persuasion that improves informed decision-making is justified; manipulation that degrades it isn't.
The TARES test: Truthfulness, Authenticity, Respect, Equity, Social responsibility — five checkpoints for any campaign.
Professional codes (PRSA): advocacy and honesty aren't opposites — ethical persuasion argues openly from real evidence.

example.code:
TARES CHECKPOINT
  T: Is every claim truthful? (not just defensible)
  A: Is the sponsor honestly identified?
  R: Does it respect audience autonomy?
  E: Is access to the debate fair?
  S: Does it serve the public interest long-term?
  One 'no' = redesign.
example.walkthrough: Run TARES on every campaign before launch. Ethics review is strategy: scandals cost more than the tactics ever gain.

pitfalls: Ends-justify-means creep — small deceptions compound into credibility collapse.
Legal-equals-ethical — lawful manipulation is still manipulation.
Client capture — 'the client wants it' doesn't transfer moral agency.
lessons.try_it: TARES-audit your current or most recent persuasive effort. Write the honest score.

lessons.title: Astroturfing and Front Groups
concepts: Astroturfing manufactures fake grassroots — paid voices posing as organic public sentiment. It's fraud, not PR.
Front groups launder sponsor identity through civic-sounding names — exposure destroys both the message and the sponsor.
Detection: identical language across 'independent' voices, opaque funding, sudden emergence around a vote or launch.
The ethical alternative: genuine coalition-building is slower but compounds — real validators can't be 'exposed.'

example.code:
SMELL TEST
  'Citizens for Sensible Policy' — who funds it? (opaque)
  40 op-eds, identical talking points (coordinated)
  Formed 3 weeks before the vote (timing)
  Verdict: astroturf until proven otherwise.
example.walkthrough: If your tactic requires hiding the sponsor, it's not strategy — it's a scandal in waiting.

pitfalls: 'Everyone does it' — the exposure asymmetry punishes you, not everyone.
Partial disclosure — 'supported by industry partners' still launders.
Short-term thinking — astroturf wins votes and loses the organization.
lessons.try_it: Investigate one advocacy group's funding. Report what you find.

lessons.title: Transparency in the Digital Age
concepts: Disclosure is the floor: sponsored content, paid endorsers, and material connections must be labeled — FTC rules and platform policies agree.
Beyond legal: proactive transparency ('here's who funded this and why') builds the trust that disclosure merely preserves.
Dark patterns in persuasion — hidden unsubscribe, false urgency, confirm-shaming — trade short-term conversion for long-term contempt.
The record is permanent: every digital tactic is screenshot-able. Design as if exposure is certain, because eventually it is.

example.code:
TRANSPARENCY LADDER
  1. Legal minimum: label sponsorship (required)
  2. Proactive: explain funding and motives upfront
  3. Structural: publish methods, data, and conflicts
  4. Cultural: invite scrutiny as proof of confidence
  Climb as high as the stakes warrant.
example.walkthrough: Transparency is a competitive advantage now: in a low-trust environment, the visibly honest actor stands out.

pitfalls: Minimum-viable disclosure — buried hashtags and 6-point font.
Dark patterns for metrics — the conversion isn't worth the contempt.
Assuming ephemerality — stories expire, screenshots don't.
lessons.try_it: Audit your digital touchpoints against the ladder. Where are you below level 2?

lessons.title: The Advocate's Responsibility
concepts: The advocate's paradox: you serve the client's interests AND the public's right to honest discourse — both, not either.
Refusing unethical work is a business strategy: the practitioners who last are the ones who can be trusted.
Whistleblowing calculus: when a client demands deception, the professional's duty to the public overrides the duty to the client.
Legacy test: 'would I defend this tactic publicly, with my name on it?' — if not, don't do it anonymously either.

example.code:
THE REFUSAL SCRIPT
  'I can't execute that tactic — it would work once and cost us permanently.
   Here's what we can do instead that achieves the goal honestly...'
  Always pair refusal with an ethical alternative. 'No' without 'instead' loses the client.
example.walkthrough: Your reputation is the only asset that compounds across clients. Spend it carefully.

pitfalls: Client-is-always-right — the professional's judgment is the product.
Silent compliance — executing without objection is endorsement.
Short engagements, long consequences — the tactic outlives the contract.
lessons.try_it: Write your personal red lines: three tactics you will never execute, with reasons.

lessons.title: Computational Propaganda
concepts: Bots, cyborgs, and coordinated networks manufacture the appearance of grassroots consensus — computational propaganda industrializes astroturf.
The IRA playbook: pose as domestic activists on both sides, inflame divisions, suppress turnout — the goal is chaos, not conversion.
Coordination signals: synchronized posting, identical text, inauthentic follower patterns, and narrative pivots too fast for organic spread.
Platform responses (takedowns, labels) lag behind operations — detection is an arms race, not a solved problem.

example.code:
COORDINATION CHECKLIST
  ☐ Posts within seconds across accounts?
  ☐ Identical/near-identical text?
  ☐ Follower/following ratios inhuman?
  ☐ Narrative pivot faster than news cycle?
  ☐ Account ages cluster around events?
  3+ checks = investigate as operation.
example.walkthrough: Apply the checklist before amplifying any viral political content. Virality is the attack surface.

pitfalls: Treating all viral content as organic — coordination is now the default hypothesis.
Only looking for foreign ops — domestic computational propaganda is larger.
Platform labels as truth — labels are delayed and gamed; do your own analysis.
lessons.try_it: Run the checklist on one viral political post today. Document the score.

lessons.title: Microtargeting and Dark Ads
concepts: Microtargeting segments audiences into thousands of slivers, each receiving tailored — often contradictory — messages invisible to others.
Dark ads: paid content visible only to targets, evading press scrutiny and opponent response — the end of the shared public sphere.
Psychographic targeting (OCEAN models) claims to predict persuasion from likes — efficacy debated, but the attempt reshapes campaigning regardless.
Regulatory response: ad libraries and transparency rules are partial — enforcement lags and cross-border buys evade.

example.code:
DARK AD ANATOMY
  Same candidate, three audiences:
  → Suburban parents: 'safe schools' ad
  → Urban youth: 'justice reform' ad
  → Rural voters: 'tradition' ad
  Contradictory promises, zero shared record.
  Democracy needs a common text; dark ads shred it.
example.walkthrough: When analyzing digital campaigns, always ask: what are the other segments seeing? The visible ad is never the whole campaign.

pitfalls: Judging a campaign by its public ads — the real campaign is in the dark.
Assuming microtargeting is mind control — it's optimization, powerful but bounded.
Ignoring the democratic cost — contradictory promises corrode accountability.
lessons.try_it: Look up a candidate in a public ad library. Compare segments — find one contradiction.

lessons.title: Deepfakes and Synthetic Media
concepts: Generative AI collapses the cost of convincing fakes — video, audio, and text that defeat casual verification.
The liar's dividend: as fakes proliferate, real evidence becomes deniable — 'that's AI-generated' becomes the universal defense.
Detection: provenance standards (C2PA), forensic artifacts, and behavioral inconsistency — no single detector is reliable.
Response protocol: slow down, check provenance, triangulate sources, and never amplify unverified synthetic content.

example.code:
SYNTHETIC MEDIA PROTOCOL
  1. Pause — virality is the delivery mechanism
  2. Provenance — C2PA data? source history?
  3. Triangulate — do independent sources confirm?
  4. Forensics — artifacts, inconsistencies?
  5. If unverified: do not share. Period.
example.walkthrough: The protocol's last step is the whole defense: unverified synthetic content dies in darkness, spreads in sharing.

pitfalls: Sharing to 'warn' about fakes — the share is the vector.
Trusting detectors absolutely — it's an arms race; detectors lag generators.
The liar's dividend trap — demanding impossible proof for real evidence.
lessons.try_it: Find C2PA/provenance info on three images you share this week. Note how often it's absent.

lessons.title: Platform Governance and Content Moderation
concepts: Platforms govern speech at scale through a mix of AI classifiers, human reviewers, and policy teams — with error rates in the millions daily.
The Santa Clara Principles: transparency (numbers), notice (tell the user), appeal (real review) — the baseline for legitimate moderation.
Deplatforming works on reach but not belief — removal reduces spread while potentially hardening adherents; plan for the trade-off.
Regulatory models diverge: US (Section 230, private ordering), EU (DSA, due diligence), authoritarian (state control) — know which regime you're in.

example.code:
MODERATION AUDIT QUESTIONS
  ☐ Published enforcement numbers?
  ☐ Notice with specific reason given?
  ☐ Meaningful appeal available?
  ☐ Consistent across viewpoints?
  ☐ Independent oversight exists?
  Legitimacy requires yeses.
example.walkthrough: Evaluate moderation systems by process legitimacy, not by whether you like the outcomes.

pitfalls: Outcome-only evaluation — legitimate process can produce disagreeable calls.
Ignoring scale — human review of billions of posts is impossible; design for it.
US-centrism — the DSA and other regimes change the rules; know the jurisdiction.
lessons.try_it: Audit one platform against the Santa Clara Principles. Publish the scorecard.

lessons.title: Classical Rhetoric: Ethos, Pathos, Logos
concepts: Ethos (character): the audience must trust the speaker — credentials, goodwill, and shared values establish it before arguments begin.
Pathos (emotion): emotion moves people to act — stories, vivid language, and moral urgency convert understanding into motion.
Logos (reason): evidence and structure convince the mind — data, mechanisms, and logical sequence for audiences that scrutinize.
The hierarchy: ethos gates (distrusted speakers aren't heard), pathos moves (emotion drives action), logos justifies (reason defends the decision).

example.code:
SPEECH TRIAGE
  Opening: ethos — 'why trust me on this' (60s)
  Body: pathos — the story that makes it matter (3 min)
  Close: logos — the evidence that it's true (2 min)
  Order matters: trust → feeling → proof.
example.walkthrough: Diagnose weak rhetoric by the missing leg: distrusted (ethos), unmoving (pathos), or unconvincing (logos).

pitfalls: Leading with logos to hostile audiences — untrusted speakers' data gets dismissed.
Pure pathos — moves people briefly, collapses under scrutiny.
Ignoring ethos — the best argument from a distrusted source fails.
lessons.try_it: Score your last persuasive effort on all three legs. Which was weakest?

lessons.title: Metaphor and Narrative
concepts: Metaphors are cognitive frames: 'argument is war' vs 'argument is dance' produces different behaviors — choose metaphors that serve your goal.
Narrative structure (hero, struggle, resolution) is the most persuasive form known — policy wrapped in story beats policy as bullet points.
The controlling metaphor test: does your metaphor illuminate or constrain? 'War on drugs' justified militarization; metaphors have casualties.
Re-metaphoring is reframing at depth: change the governing metaphor and the conclusions change with it.

example.code:
METAPHOR AUDIT
  Current: 'fighting' climate change (war metaphor → enemies, sacrifice, victory)
  Alternative: 'healing' the climate (care metaphor → stewardship, patience)
  Different metaphors, different policies, different politics.
  Choose deliberately.
example.walkthrough: Audit the governing metaphors in your issue. Then ask: who benefits from this metaphor, and what would change with another?

pitfalls: Dead metaphors unexamined — 'war on' everything militarizes by default.
Story without data — narrative persuades, evidence sustains.
Mixed metaphors — competing frames confuse; pick one and hold it.
lessons.try_it: Identify the governing metaphor of one debate. Propose an alternative and trace its different conclusions.

lessons.title: Debate Tactics and Fallacies
concepts: Know the fallacies to spot them, not just to name them: ad hominem, strawman, false dilemma, slippery slope, appeal to authority — recognition is defense.
The Gish gallop: flooding with weak arguments so rebuttal can't keep up — counter by picking the strongest and demolishing it, then noting the pattern.
Sealioning: bad-faith demands for evidence that exhaust — set the evidence standard once, then decline the infinite regress.
Steel-manning: state the opponent's best case before refuting it — it disarms, earns credibility, and makes your rebuttal devastating.

example.code:
FALLACY RESPONSE KIT
  Ad hominem → 'address the argument, not me'
  Strawman → 'that's not my position; it is...'
  Gish gallop → 'of those twelve, the strongest is X — here's why it fails...'
  Sealioning → 'evidence standard set; moving on'
  Always steel-man first.
example.walkthrough: The goal isn't winning internet arguments — it's keeping your reasoning clean under pressure.

pitfalls: Fallacy-labeling as dismissal — naming isn't refuting; engage the substance.
Gish-gallop panic — don't chase twelve; kill the strongest.
Never steel-manning — it costs little and buys devastating credibility.
lessons.try_it: Take an opponent's argument. Steel-man it in three sentences before critiquing.

lessons.title: Speechwriting Essentials
concepts: Structure: hook (attention), need (problem), vision (solution), ask (action) — every persuasive speech follows this arc.
The rule of three: triads are memorable ('government of the people, by the people, for the people') — organize key points in threes.
Soundbites are engineered: short, vivid, repeatable — write the quote you want reported, don't hope reporters find one.
Delivery is half the message: pace, pause, and eye contact carry the words — rehearse out loud, never just on paper.

example.code:
SPEECH SKELETON
  Hook (30s): story or startling fact
  Need (2min): the problem, made vivid
  Vision (2min): the solution, in threes
  Ask (30s): specific action, clear and easy
  Soundbite: the one line for the headline — write it first.
example.walkthrough: Write the soundbite first, then build the speech to earn it.

pitfalls: No ask — inspiration without action is entertainment.
No triads — unstructured lists are forgotten.
Paper-only prep — unrehearsed delivery undermines good writing.
lessons.try_it: Write a 5-minute speech skeleton on your issue. Include the engineered soundbite.

lessons.title: Crystallizing Public Opinion: The Counsel's Playbook
concepts: Bernays' 1923 book Crystallizing Public Opinion invented a new profession: the 'public relations counsel' — part journalist, part social scientist, part lawyer — who advises the client on what the public will accept and how to shape that acceptance.

The counsel's method starts with research: Bernays surveyed and sampled opinion before opinion polling was standard practice, then designed the message and the event around what the research revealed about the audience's existing desires.

Instead of buying ad space, the counsel creates circumstances: staged events, endorsements, and newsworthy acts that reporters cover as news, so the message arrives with the press's credibility attached rather than the advertiser's discount.
Two-way adjustment: Bernays insisted the counsel sometimes tells the client to change its behavior, not just its messaging — a counsel who only flatters the client is a press agent, not a strategist.

example.code:
A COUNSEL'S PLAN (outline)
  1. RESEARCH: What does the target public already want, fear, admire?
  2. ADJUST: What must the client change so the message is true?
  3. EVENT: What overt act will the press cover as news?
  4. CARRIERS: Which trusted third parties will carry it?
  5. MEASURE: Did attitudes move? (sales, polls, coverage tone)
example.walkthrough: This outline is the skeleton under every Bernays campaign in the case-studies domain: research first, event second, third parties third, measurement last. Run any campaign through these five steps and you can spot which step was skipped when one fails.

pitfalls: Treating 'counsel' as a fancy word for publicist — the counsel advises on policy and behavior, not just publicity.
Skipping the research step and staging an event for an audience you have not studied — the classic cause of dead campaigns.
Forgetting two-way adjustment: a message the client's own behavior contradicts will collapse on contact with reality.
lessons.try_it: Pick a real organization you know. Draft a five-line counsel's plan for it using the outline above — especially step 2, the hard truth you would tell the client.

lessons.title: The Engineering of Consent (1947)
concepts: In his 1947 essay 'The Engineering of Consent,' Bernays argued that democratic leadership requires deliberately shaping public attitudes with social-science methods — engineering consent, he claimed, is what makes large-scale democracy workable at all.

The context was postwar anxiety: propaganda had just been the weapon of fascist regimes, and Bernays was trying to rehabilitate planned persuasion as compatible with — even necessary to — democracy rather than its enemy.

The democratic paradox at the essay's core: Bernays claimed the engineer of consent respects citizens' ultimate judgment and merely organizes the conditions of choice, while critics replied that engineering bypasses the very deliberation democracy is supposed to be.

The phrase outlived the essay: 'engineering of consent' became both a manual title for political communicators and a warning label used by media critics — the same words, opposite moral charges, depending on who says them.

example.code:
THE PARADOX, STATED PLAINLY
  Bernays' claim:  Mass democracy needs organized persuasion to function.
  Critics' reply:  Organized persuasion replaces the citizen with the managed subject.
  The test:       Would the technique survive full disclosure?
  Persuasion that survives disclosure = democratic. What must hide = manipulation.
example.walkthrough: That four-line test is the portable tool: apply it to any campaign — commercial, political, or your own — and it separates the Bernays you can defend from the Bernays you should fear.

pitfalls: Reading the essay as a confession of manipulation — Bernays genuinely believed he was describing democratic leadership, which is what makes the paradox hard.
Quoting 'engineering of consent' as if the phrase settles the ethics — it names the problem; it does not solve it.
Missing the postwar context: the essay is an answer to 'was all propaganda fascist?' — and its answer is 'no, if disclosed and deliberated.'
lessons.try_it: Take one current political ad you have seen. Run the disclosure test: if every technique in it were printed underneath, would it still work? Write your verdict in two sentences.

lessons.title: Bernays' Legacy: The Critics' Case
concepts: Bernays built directly on Walter Lippmann's Public Opinion (1922): people act on 'the pictures in their heads' — stereotypes and simplifications — and whoever shapes those pictures shapes behavior without issuing a single order.

Later critics extended the charge: once Bernays-style techniques were institutionalized in PR firms and political consultancies, the 'engineering of consent' became the normal operating procedure of elite communication — management of news rather than participation in debate.

The case studies supply the prosecution's exhibits: Torches of Freedom sold women's liberation to sell cigarettes; the United Fruit work helped topple a government. The techniques were brilliant; the question is what they were pointed at.

The counter-legacy is media literacy itself: teaching citizens the counsel's playbook — third-party laundering, manufactured events, loaded framing — so the audience can spot the engineering in real time. This course is Bernays' legacy turned inside out.

example.code:
THE CRITICS' SYLLOGISM
  1. People act on pictures in their heads (Lippmann).
  2. Those pictures can be engineered at scale (Bernays).
  3. Therefore whoever engineers the pictures governs without governing.
  The defense:  an audience trained to see the engineering is no longer governable that way.
example.walkthrough: That is why this bootcamp pairs every technique with a literacy defense: the goal is not to mint better engineers of consent but citizens who cannot be engineered without their knowledge.

pitfalls: Treating criticism of Bernays as criticism of persuasion itself — the target is concealed, large-scale attitude management, not honest argument.
Assuming the critics 'won' and the techniques died — they professionalized and digitized instead; see the digital-propaganda domain.
Reading Torches of Freedom as feminist history without the American Tobacco client in the frame — the client is always in the frame.
lessons.try_it: Write the critics' one-paragraph case against one Bernays campaign of your choice — then write the one-paragraph defense a PR counsel would offer. Which is stronger?

lessons.title: The Influence Operation as a System: Sender to Feedback
concepts: Every influence campaign is a five-stage flow: SENDER (client + counsel) designs the message, CHANNELS (press, events, third-party carriers) transmit it, AUDIENCE segments receive and decode it, and FEEDBACK (coverage tone, polls, sales, behavior) returns to the sender for adjustment.

Each handoff is a failure point: the sender can misread the audience, the channels can refuse the story (gatekeeping), the audience can decode oppositionally, and the feedback can measure the wrong thing — a campaign dies at its weakest handoff, not its weakest idea.

Earned media is the system's scarcest resource: unlike paid ads, coverage must be earned through newsworthiness, which is why Bernays engineered events rather than buying space — he was hacking the channel stage of the system.

Feedback closes the loop: polls and coverage monitoring tell the counsel which stage is underperforming, and the campaign is re-tuned mid-flight — modern digital campaigns run this loop hourly; Bernays ran it weekly by clipping newspapers.

example.code:
THE INFLUENCE SYSTEM (flow)
  SENDER --design--> CHANNELS --transmit--> AUDIENCE --decode--> BEHAVIOR
     ^                                                              |
     |______________________ FEEDBACK ______________________________|
  Failure diagnosis: find the handoff where expected output diverges from actual.
  - No coverage?      CHANNEL stage: not newsworthy enough.
  - Coverage, no move? AUDIENCE stage: wrong frame or messenger.
  - Moved, then died?  FEEDBACK stage: measured vanity, missed backlash.
example.walkthrough: This diagnostic is the systems lens for every case study in this course: when you read a campaign, draw the five stages and mark where it broke or where it soared.

pitfalls: Treating the campaign as a single 'message' — the message is one stage; the system is five.
Blaming the audience when the channel stage failed — 'they didn't get it' usually means the press never carried it or the frame was wrong.
Measuring only the final behavior and skipping stage-by-stage feedback — then you cannot diagnose, only mourn.
lessons.try_it: Draw the five-stage flow for the Torches of Freedom campaign. Label each handoff with what Bernays actually did there.

lessons.title: Feedback Loops and Second-Order Effects in Influence Systems
concepts: Reinforcing loops amplify: press coverage builds credibility, which earns more coverage, which builds more credibility — Bernays' campaigns were designed to ignite this loop so the message would propagate without further spending.

Balancing loops resist: backlash, audience fatigue, and opponent counter-framing push back against the message — every reinforcing loop eventually meets one, and campaigns that plan only for amplification are blindsided when the balancing loop engages.

Second-order effects escape the plan: Torches of Freedom normalized smoking for a generation of women (a public-health effect far beyond cigarette sales), and the United Fruit campaign helped enable a coup (a geopolitical effect far beyond bananas) — the system always produces more than the sender intended.

Systems ethics means mapping the full loop before launch: who absorbs the externalities, which balancing loops might engage, and what happens if the reinforcing loop overshoots — the counsel's responsibility does not end at the client's objective.

example.code:
LOOP MAP (template)
  Reinforcing: coverage -> credibility -> more coverage (plan for ignition)
  Balancing:   backlash / fatigue / counter-frame (plan for resistance)
  Second-order: effects on non-target audiences and systems (plan for externalities)
  Ask before launch: What if this works TOO well? Who pays for the overshoot?
example.walkthrough: That last question is the one Bernays' clients rarely asked — and the one the pr-ethics domain keeps asking on their behalf.

pitfalls: Drawing only the intended causal chain — the system's real behavior lives in the loops you did not draw.
Treating backlash as a messaging failure rather than a balancing loop — it is structural, and it needs a structural response (address the grievance), not a louder message.
Ignoring second-order effects because 'that wasn't the goal' — systems do not grade on intentions.
lessons.try_it: Pick any campaign you admire. Sketch its reinforcing loop, its likely balancing loop, and one second-order effect nobody planned. Two sentences each.

lessons.title: Torches of Freedom (1929)
concepts: The context: in the 1920s a taboo held that respectable women did not smoke in public — which meant half the population was a closed market. Bernays' client, the American Tobacco Company, wanted that market opened without advertising against a moral taboo.

The operation: Bernays hired fashionable young women to march in the 1929 New York Easter parade smoking cigarettes, tipped off photographers in advance, and supplied the frame — 'Torches of Freedom' — fusing the cigarette to the women's emancipation movement.

The mechanism: the press covered it as news about feminism, not as advertising about tobacco. The message rode on the movement's credibility, the debutantes served as third-party carriers, and the paying client stayed invisible.

The aftermath: the taboo cracked, women's smoking rose, and the campaign became the textbook manufactured event — studied ever since as proof that news can be engineered when you understand what the press cannot ignore.

example.code:
DISSECTION: TORCHES
  Client (hidden): American Tobacco Company — expand the women's market
  Carriers: debutantes as 'feminists,' not salespeople
  Event: Easter parade — cameras already present, tipped in advance
  Frame: emancipation — product welded to a genuine cause
  Channel: press covers it as NEWS (earned, not paid)
  Result: taboo broken; smoking = liberation in the public picture
example.walkthrough: That six-line dissection is the template for every case study in this domain: client, carriers, event, frame, channel, result. Memorize the template; the campaigns change, the anatomy does not.

pitfalls: Remembering the stunt but forgetting the hidden client — the client is the most important line of the dissection.
Calling it 'feminist history' without the tobacco frame — the cause was real; its use as a cigarette wrapper was the technique.
Thinking the lesson is 'stage parades' — the lesson is cause fusion plus earned media; the parade was just 1929's feed.
lessons.try_it: Dissect a modern influencer stunt using the six-line template. Which line is hardest to fill in — and what does that tell you?

lessons.title: The Bacon-and-Eggs Breakfast Campaign
concepts: The assignment: a bacon producer wanted Americans to eat a heavier breakfast. Direct advertising saying 'eat more bacon' would have been ignored — so Bernays manufactured authority instead.

The operation: Bernays commissioned a survey of physicians asking whether a hearty breakfast was better than a light one. The question was engineered — 'hearty' pointed straight at bacon and eggs — and 4,500 physicians dutifully endorsed the hearty breakfast.

The mechanism: the press reported 'doctors say hearty breakfast is best,' and the physicians' credibility laundered the bacon company's commercial goal. Nobody lied about the numbers; the question did the work.

The lesson: third-party authority is most powerful when it looks independent. The literacy defense is provenance — who commissioned the survey, how was the question worded, and who profits from the answer.

example.code:
DISSECTION: BACON
  Client (hidden): bacon producer — sell a heavier breakfast
  Carriers: 4,500 physicians — credible, apparently independent
  Instrument: survey with an engineered question ('hearty vs light')
  Channel: press reports 'doctors say...' as health news
  Result: breakfast habits shift; bacon sales rise
  Tell: the question's wording made the desired answer inevitable
example.walkthrough: Note what was NOT falsified: the doctors really answered, the count was real. Manufactured authority rarely forges data — it engineers the question. That is why provenance checks beat fact-checks here.

pitfalls: Assuming the survey was faked — it was not; the manipulation was in the question design, which is harder to spot.
