Trusting 'studies show' without asking who commissioned the study — the most expensive literacy failure in this domain.
Thinking this is ancient history — commissioned surveys with engineered questions remain a staple of modern PR.
lessons.try_it: Find a 'studies show' headline online. Trace it: who funded the study, what was the exact question or method? Report what you find.

lessons.title: The Dixie Cup Campaign
concepts: The assignment: sell disposable paper cups. The obstacle: people shared cups at public fountains and offices without a second thought — there was no demand for a solution to a problem nobody felt.

The operation: Bernays reframed the shared cup as a vector of disease and the paper cup as the sanitary, modern, morally responsible choice — piggybacking on genuine public-health anxiety rather than inventing a fear from nothing.

The mechanism: institutions — schools, offices — adopted disposables as hygiene policy, becoming third-party validators. Once the paper cup was the 'clean' choice, the shared cup became the shameful one; moral framing did the selling.

The lesson: fear piggybacking borrows a real anxiety and positions the product as the responsible answer. The literacy check is proportionality — was the danger as large as the campaign made it feel, and who profited from the size of the feeling?

example.code:
DISSECTION: DIXIE
  Client: paper-cup maker — create demand where none existed
  Fuel: genuine anxiety about disease from shared cups
  Frame: disposable = sanitary and moral; shared = dirty and backward
  Validators: institutions adopting disposables as policy
  Result: throwaway habit normalized as hygiene virtue
  Check: proportionality — how big was the risk vs. how big it felt?
example.walkthrough: Compare with Torches: same system, different fuel — aspiration there, anxiety here. The fuel determines the defense: check the cause's authenticity for aspiration campaigns, check the fear's proportionality for anxiety campaigns.

pitfalls: Dismissing it because the cups really were more sanitary — the technique is not the product's merit but the scale of the fear manufactured around it.
Missing the institutional validators — schools and offices adopting the cup did more selling than any ad.
Forgetting that moral framing ('clean vs dirty') outlasts the campaign — the habit persisted for a century.
lessons.try_it: Name a modern product sold with moral framing around health or cleanliness. Run the proportionality check on its core fear.

lessons.title: Light's Golden Jubilee (1929)
concepts: The assignment: the electric industry wanted national prestige and goodwill. Bernays' answer was not an ad campaign but a national celebration — the 50th anniversary of Edison's incandescent lamp, October 1929.

The operation: weeks of events culminating in a ceremony with the President, honoring Edison at Dearborn. The press covered it as national history, not industry promotion — the scale made coverage obligatory.

The mechanism: anniversary-jacking. A milestone supplies the news peg, the honoree's prestige (Edison, the presidency) transfers to the sponsors, and the pageantry wraps the industry's message in celebration. Nobody reports 'industry buys goodwill'; they report the Jubilee.

The lesson: borrowed prestige is the highest-leverage carrier — greater than any celebrity, because institutions and history outrank individuals. The literacy defense is the funding question: whose anniversary is it really, and what is being sold inside the celebration?

example.code:
DISSECTION: JUBILEE
  Clients: electric industry — prestige and goodwill at national scale
  Peg: 50th anniversary of the incandescent lamp (calendar as newsworthiness)
  Prestige donors: Edison's legacy, the presidency, national history
  Channel: weeks of earned coverage — too big to ignore
  Result: industry basks in reflected glory; message = celebration
  Tell: the sponsors' names sit quietly inside the pageantry
example.walkthrough: This is the largest-scale manufactured event in the Bernays canon — proof the technique scales from a parade stunt to a national ritual. Scale changes the channel math: at some size, coverage stops being earned and becomes inevitable.

pitfalls: Thinking anniversaries are 'natural' news — this one was manufactured by the industry that benefited from it.
Missing the prestige transfer — Edison's glow, not the industry's merits, did the persuading.
Assuming only 1929 could do this — every sponsored 'national day of' and anniversary celebration since uses the same playbook.
lessons.try_it: Find a modern sponsored anniversary, awareness day, or jubilee. Identify the sponsor inside the celebration and the message it carries.

lessons.title: United Fruit and Guatemala (1954)
concepts: The assignment: the United Fruit Company faced land reform in Guatemala under President Arbenz that threatened its holdings. Bernays was retained to turn U.S. opinion — and therefore U.S. policy — against the Arbenz government.

The operation: press junkets brought friendly American reporters to see the 'communist threat' firsthand; land reform was reframed as Moscow-directed subversion; every company setback became evidence of a Red beachhead in the hemisphere.

The mechanism: geopolitical PR — the same influence system as the commercial campaigns (sender, channels, audience, feedback), but with the audience being policymakers and the behavior being intervention. The frame 'communism' did the work that 'emancipation' did for cigarettes.

The aftermath: in 1954 a CIA-backed coup toppled Arbenz, beginning decades of instability. The campaign is the canon's darkest case — the proof that influence techniques pointed at governments produce second-order effects no client ever prices: the externality was a country's future.

example.code:
DISSECTION: GUATEMALA
  Client: United Fruit — protect land holdings from reform
  Carriers: friendly reporters on junkets; 'experts' on communism
  Frame: land reform = Moscow-directed subversion (red-baiting)
  Channel: U.S. press coverage shaping the climate for intervention
  Result: 1954 coup; Arbenz falls
  Externality: decades of Guatemalan instability — never on the invoice
example.walkthrough: This case is why the systems-anatomy domain teaches second-order effects and why pr-ethics teaches the advocate's responsibility: the techniques are neutral, their targets and externalities are not. Every counsel should study this before accepting a geopolitical assignment.

pitfalls: Treating it as 'just PR' — the techniques were PR; the output was regime change, and the analysis must hold both.
Blaming only the CIA — the campaign manufactured the consent the operation needed; consent-engineering was load-bearing.
Reading it as ancient history — state and corporate actors still run this exact playbook; only the channels updated.
lessons.try_it: Write the counsel's memo declining a modern equivalent of this assignment. State the line, the foreseeable harm, and the professional doctrine behind the refusal.

simulations.title: Name the Technique
simulations.brief: A 1929 soap advertisement is doing several things at once. Diagnose which persuasion technique is doing the heavy lifting.

steps.symptom: An ad shows a famous surgeon holding a bar of soap. No medical claim is made — just the surgeon's face, the soap, and the word 'Purity'.
evidence: "Purity — the choice of those who know."
Surgeon in white coat, hospital corridor backdrop
None — the surgeon is a paid endorser, unstated
options: Plain-folks appeal — the ad is positioning soap as ordinary
Transfer / prestige association: the surgeon's authority is transferred to the soap without any logical connection
Bandwagon — the ad claims everyone already buys it
steps.explain: Transfer moves prestige from one symbol (the surgeon) to an unrelated product. The defense is the same every time: ask what the authority actually knows about the product.

steps.symptom: A campaign leaflet repeats one phrase — 'the people's choice' — on every page, in every speech, for six months.
evidence: None — repetition stands in for proof
options: Card stacking — selective facts are being arranged
The illusory truth effect via relentless repetition: repeated statements feel truer regardless of evidence
Glittering generality — vague virtue words are doing the work
steps.explain: Repetition manufactures familiarity, and familiarity is misread as truth. Bernays understood this as engineering: say it everywhere, and the public finishes the argument for you.

steps.symptom: You must brief a community group on defending themselves. Which defense generalizes across all these techniques?
evidence: One habit they can actually practice daily
Works against transfer, repetition, and card stacking alike
options: Memorize a list of every known propaganda technique
Source-checking habit: who benefits, what evidence is shown vs. implied, and what the authority actually knows
Avoid all advertising and political messaging entirely
steps.explain: Media literacy is a procedure, not a blacklist: who benefits, what's evidenced versus implied, and whether the invoked authority has relevant knowledge. That one habit answers every technique.

simulations.debrief: Propaganda analysis is diagnostic work: name the technique, trace what it substitutes for evidence, then install the counter-habit. Bernays engineered consent; the defense is engineered skepticism.

simulations.title: The Press Agent's Dilemma
simulations.brief: It's 1924. A tobacco client wants you to make smoking fashionable for women. Your press-agent skills are in demand — your conscience is not consulted. Decide.

steps.text: 1924. The client: 'Make cigarettes respectable for women. Budget is unlimited.' You know the health evidence is thin but the paycheck is enormous. Your first move?

choices.label: Take the account and plan the 'Torches of Freedom' style stunt — emotion over evidence
choices.feedback: You stage a parade where debutantes light up as symbols of emancipation. It works brilliantly — and you have engineered consent for a product you privately doubt.

choices.label: Take the account but insist on factual, non-manipulative copy
choices.feedback: The client smiles and hires someone else who won't insist. The campaign happens anyway, without you.

choices.label: Decline the account and document why — then study the techniques from the outside
choices.feedback: You lose the fee but keep the clear view. From the sidelines you can see the whole machine: third-party authorities, staged events, manufactured news.

steps.text: The stunt makes front pages nationwide. Sales surge. A journalist asks you point-blank: 'Was this news, or advertising?' How do you answer?

choices.label: 'It was a genuine expression of women's liberation.'
choices.feedback: The lie compounds. You have now manufactured both the event and its meaning — the full Bernays playbook, and its full moral cost.

choices.label: 'It was a publicity event we organized.'
choices.feedback: Honesty after the fact doesn't unring the bell, but it stops the next deception. Rare — and noted.

steps.text: From the sidelines you watch the campaign roll out: planted experts, staged 'news', repetition. A newspaper editor asks you to explain how it works — on the record. What do you do?

choices.label: Explain the machinery publicly — third-party technique, event staging, repetition
choices.feedback: You convert inside knowledge into public defense. The editor runs the exposé; readers learn to ask who staged the 'news'.

choices.label: Stay quiet — the industry is small and you may want back in
choices.feedback: Silence is a choice with a price: the machine runs unopposed, and you watched it happen.

steps.text: As an outside analyst you catalog the campaign's anatomy: the third-party authorities, the staged event, the repetition cycle. A university asks you to teach media literacy. What's the core lesson?

choices.label: 'Every message is manipulation — trust nothing.'
choices.feedback: Cynicism is not literacy; it leaves students defenseless against the next well-made lie, because they've stopped evaluating.

choices.label: 'Ask who staged it, who benefits, and what evidence would change your mind.'
choices.feedback: You teach the procedure, not the paranoia. Students leave able to dissect any campaign — including the ones they'll meet tomorrow.

simulations.debrief: The historical record is the textbook: third-party authorities, staged events, repetition. Studying the engineering of consent from the analyst's chair — and teaching the counter-procedure — is the independent-study payoff.

simulations.title: Anatomy of a Campaign
simulations.brief: Order the five stages of a classic Bernays-style public relations campaign, from research to reinforcement.

steps.context: A 1920s-style campaign to shift public opinion. Put the stages in the order the engineering actually runs.
items: Research the public's existing desires, fears, and group leaders
Recruit third-party authorities to carry the message credibly
Stage a newsworthy event that dramatizes the message
Amplify coverage through repetition across every channel
Reinforce: fold the new attitude into identity ('people like us do this')

simulations.debrief: Research first (find the latent desire), authority second (borrow credibility), event third (manufacture news), repetition fourth (make it feel true), identity last (make it feel like self). Recognizing the sequence is the first step to interrupting it.

simulations.title: Feed Audit: Find the Manipulation
simulations.brief: A 'neutral' news aggregator's ranking config is doing persuasion work. Find the 3 manipulative settings.

steps.config:
# ranker.conf — 'neutral news aggregator'
boost_paid_placement = 3.0        # line 2
label_sponsored = false         # line 3
outrage_weight = 2.5            # line 4
recency_decay = normal          # line 5
diversity_penalty = 1.8         # line 6
fact_check_badge = enabled      # line 7
engagement_loop = infinite      # line 8

issues.description: Paid placement boosted 3x — advertisers buy the top of your 'neutral' feed.
issues.fix: boost_paid_placement = 1.0, or remove paid content from the news ranking entirely.

issues.description: Sponsored labels disabled — paid persuasion is presented as organic news.
Outrage weighted 2.5x — the algorithm amplifies whatever angers you most, the oldest manipulation trick in the book, now automated.
issues.fix: outrage_weight = 1.0; rank by relevance and recency, not anger.

simulations.debrief: Bernays needed press agents; the modern machine needs only a config file. Lines 5–7 are defensible (recency, diversity, fact-check badges); the three flagged lines are consent engineering running as code.

simulations.title: Amplify or Expose
simulations.brief: A viral video is moving markets. Your 200k-follower account can amplify it — or dissect it. The video's claims are unverified.

steps.text: A slick 90-second video claims a household product causes illness. 2M views in 6 hours. The 'expert' is unnamed, the study uncited. Your followers are asking what you think. First move?

choices.label: Share it with 'THIS IS HUGE' — engagement will be massive
choices.feedback: You become a node in the amplification network. If the claims are false, you've laundered them with your credibility.

choices.label: Post a thread dissecting it: unnamed expert, uncited study, emotional editing
choices.feedback: You apply the procedure publicly — who benefits, what's evidenced vs. implied. Some followers call you a shill; most learn the method.

choices.label: Wait 24 hours before saying anything
choices.feedback: Patience is a legitimate tactic — but silence while it spreads is also a position. The window for inoculation narrows hourly.

steps.text: Your share added 400k views. A fact-checker now confirms the video's core claim is false — and traces its funding to a competitor of the product. Damage control?

choices.label: Delete quietly and move on
choices.feedback: The correction never reaches the 400k. Quiet deletion protects you, not the people you misled.

choices.label: Post a full correction: what you shared, why it was wrong, who funded it — with the same energy as the original share
choices.feedback: Corrections rarely travel as far, but a loud, honest one is the only ethical move. You've learned the amplifier's responsibility the hard way.

steps.text: Your thread goes modestly viral itself. A PR firm emails: 'We represent the video's creators. We'd like to discuss a partnership.' What's behind the curtain?

choices.label: Take the meeting — hear them out
choices.feedback: The meeting is the recruitment attempt: today's third-party technique is the 'independent creator partnership'. You walk in knowing exactly what it is.

choices.label: Publish the email with analysis: this is how modern third-party recruitment works
choices.feedback: You turn the recruitment attempt into the lesson. Your followers watch a Bernays technique arrive in real time — and recognize it.

simulations.debrief: The machinery Bernays built now runs at internet speed: virality replaces the parade, creators replace the debutantes. The defense hasn't changed — evidence, sources, beneficiaries — but it has to run just as fast.

terminalMissions.title: Open the Archive
terminalMissions.brief: Every investigation starts by surveying the sources. List the workspace and read the study notes.

checks.hint: Type: ls — the archive listing includes notes.txt.
Type: cat notes.txt — the notes mention grep among the essentials.

terminalMissions.success_message: Archive surveyed. Know what sources you hold before you make claims about them.

terminalMissions.title: Transcribe the Leaflet
terminalMissions.brief: Transcribe a 1929 leaflet slogan into leaflet.txt, then read it back to verify the transcription.

checks.hint: Type: echo "the people's choice" > leaflet.txt (no output on success).
Type: cat leaflet.txt — your transcribed slogan appears.

terminalMissions.success_message: Transcribed and verified. Primary sources first — commentary later.

terminalMissions.title: Count the Repetition
terminalMissions.brief: Repetition is the technique. Append the slogan three times, then measure how repetition accumulates.
objectives: Repeat the slogan into the file

checks.hint: Append again: echo "the people's choice" >> leaflet.txt — repeat it a few times.
Type: wc -l leaflet.txt — the count shows how repetition stacks.
Type: grep choice leaflet.txt — every repeated line is listed.

terminalMissions.success_message: Repetition quantified. Familiarity is not evidence — but now you can measure exactly how much familiarity was manufactured.

terminalMissions.title: Verify Document Integrity
terminalMissions.brief: Archives get tampered with. Seal your transcription with a real SHA-256 hash so any later alteration is detectable.
objectives: Hash the transcription file's key phrase

checks.hint: Type: sha256sum "people's choice" — the real hash is computed and the quoted phrase echoed back.

terminalMissions.success_message: Sealed. A hash is a commitment: alter one character of the source and the seal breaks.

terminalMissions.title: Read the Server Logs
terminalMissions.brief: A 'news' site's traffic spiked during the campaign. Read its access log edges for anomalies.

checks.hint: Type: head -n 2 logs/app.log — the log opens with the server starting.
Type: tail -n 2 logs/app.log — the tail shows the timeout error.

terminalMissions.success_message: Edges read. Anomalies live at the boundaries — what started normally and what ended badly.

terminalMissions.title: Trace the Source Domain
terminalMissions.brief: Before citing a site, check it resolves and the path to it is clean — basic source hygiene.

checks.hint: Type: dig example-news.org — the ANSWER SECTION returns its address.
Type: ping example-news.org — zero packet loss confirms the path.

terminalMissions.success_message: Source traced. 'Who published this and can I reach them' precedes 'do I believe them'.

terminalMissions.title: Audit the Environment
terminalMissions.brief: Analysts verify their own tools first. Confirm your shell environment is what you expect.
objectives: Confirm the working directory via variable expansion

checks.hint: Type: ps — this sandbox prints the environment; find HOME=/home/candidate.

terminalMissions.success_message: Environment audited. Verify the instrument before trusting the measurement — in archives as in shells.

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about the most technically difficult problem you have run into — a homelab, a broken environment, anything — and how you solved it.
points: Pick ONE problem with a real evidence trail: the symptom, what you measured, the hypothesis you tested
Show the loop: scope, observe, hypothesize, smallest safe change, validate — interviewers score the method, not just the fix
Name the tools (VM build, networking, logs) and the lesson it taught you
Close with the result in concrete terms: what works now that did not before
pitfalls: Choosing a story with no real obstacle (“I Googled it” is not a story)
Skipping validation — saying it worked without proving it
Rambling past two minutes without reaching the result

behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you dealt with a frustrated customer or user while something was broken.
points: Lead with empathy and ownership: acknowledge the impact before the technical detail
Show translation: what you told them, in their language, plus the timeline you committed to
Show judgment: the narrow fix you chose and what you refused to do (e.g., disabling the control to clear the symptom)
Close with the relationship outcome, not just the technical one
pitfalls: Badmouthing the customer to sound decisive
Promising a timeline you could not keep
Framing the user as the problem rather than the situation

points: Connect prevention to something concrete: a moment you saw detection arrive too late, or a system you hardened
Tie their model to your instincts: deny-by-default matches how you already think about trust
Show service orientation: the Cyber Hero culture rewards the 2 a.m. helper — give an example of being one
Name one forward-looking reason: Zero Trust, the MSP mission, or the bootcamp community investment
pitfalls: Generic flattery with no specifics about the company
Leading with compensation, title, or location convenience
Claiming expertise in products you have only read about — frame it as studied, not mastered
Staying vague ('I analyzed the data') instead of naming what you connected.
Skipping your own role: what did YOU see that others missed?
No outcome: what changed because you joined the dots?
points: The scattered signals and why nobody had connected them yet
The specific links you drew between them (shared host, time, infrastructure)
What the bigger picture turned out to be and what action it drove
What the experience taught you about investigating
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you connected scattered clues into a bigger picture that others had missed.

pitfalls: Claiming you fixed everything: credibility comes from trade-offs, not heroics.
Hiding the constraint: the limitation is what makes the prioritization story real.
No metric: 'better' needs a before-and-after.
points: The constraint (time, budget, staff) and the size of the backlog
How you decided what mattered most (what was reachable, what was critical)
What you did first and what you deliberately deferred
The measurable result of the prioritization
behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to prioritize risks or fixes with limited time or resources. How did you decide what came first?

pitfalls: Reciting jargon to a non-technical audience and calling it communication.
Skipping the audience's reaction: did they actually understand and act?
Making yourself the hero instead of the translator.
points: The technical finding and why it mattered
Who the audience was and what they cared about
How you reframed it (a picture, an analogy, a story)
What decision or action the audience took because they understood
behavioral.prompt: Tell me about a time you explained a complex technical finding to a non-technical audience and it changed a decision.
Tell me about a time you used automation or AI to solve a security problem.
points: The repetitive security task and what it cost in analyst time
The automation or AI approach you built and how you validated it
Measured outcome: time saved, detection gained, false positives changed
pitfalls: Describing the tool but never the validation
No measurable outcome

behavioral.prompt: Describe a time you had to decide whether to trust an automated security decision.
points: The stakes of the automated action and its blast radius
How you verified before acting (or the gate you built)
What happened and what you would automate differently next time
pitfalls: Saying you always trust the tool
No mention of blast radius or reversibility

sections.heading: Product stack
items: Allowlisting — default-deny execution control for apps, DLLs, scripts, installers
Ringfencing — constrains allowed apps: app-to-app, file, registry, network
Storage Control — USB/device policy by serial, user, file type, encryption
Elevation Control — just-in-time per-app admin, no standing rights
Network Control — host firewall; port/IP/dynamic-ACL rules; ZTNA foundation
Web Control — agent-based DNS/URL category filtering, works off-network
Cyber Hero MDR — 24/7/365 US-based response, ~60-second average
Testing Environment — one-button VDI sandbox; checks AV flags, canary files, registry changes

sections.heading: Rule strength (strongest to weakest)
items: Certificate/publisher rules — survive version updates
Hash rules — precise but break on every new version
Path rules — weakest; never in user-writable locations
Learning Mode catalogs before enforcement; Installation Mode pauses blocking — scope and time-box both

sections.heading: Terminal evidence commands
items: nmap <host> — which ports answer (22/80/443 open)
dig <name> — ANSWER SECTION with the A record
ss — listening sockets
systemctl status <svc> — unit state
journalctl -u <svc> — service logs
sha256sum <file> — real SHA-256 identity
grep <pattern> <file> — search the record
ps — what is actually running

sections.heading: Graph vocabulary
items: node — any entity tracked in the model (user, host, IP, domain, file hash, vulnerability)
edge — a labeled relationship between two nodes (logged into, resolved to, downloaded)
degree — number of edges on a node; high-degree nodes are attacker highways
centrality — how much traffic or how many paths flow through a node
directed edge — a relationship with a direction (A downloaded FROM B)
security graph — the living model of your whole environment as nodes and edges
attack graph — the subgraph of exploitable paths to your targets
knowledge graph — threat-intel indicators linked to campaigns and actors

sections.heading: Attack-graph playbook
items: inventory first — you cannot graph what you have not discovered
model flaws AND misconfigs as exploit edges
compute shortest paths to the crown jewels
find the choke point (highest betweenness on those paths)
break the path: patch, segment, or remove the edge
re-scan and re-run the graph to prove the path is gone
never trust yesterday's graph — redeployments redraw the map

sections.heading: Zero Trust + graphs
items: never trust, always verify — re-evaluate every access decision
assume breach — treat unexpected edges as hostile until proven otherwise
microsegmentation — allow-list approved edges, alert on new ones
ReBAC — policies are path queries on the identity graph
continuous verification — device/location/behavior edges change, trust follows
anomalous edge — a first-seen connection between strangers is the classic signal

sections.heading: ML detection vocabulary
items: Supervised learning — learns from labeled examples; strong on known threats, blind to novel ones
Unsupervised learning — finds structure without labels; clustering and dimensionality reduction
Anomaly detection — models 'normal' and flags deviations; the workhorse for novel threats
UEBA — user and entity behavior analytics: per-user baselines plus peer-group comparison
Feature engineering — encoding raw logs into model inputs (login velocity, rare processes, domain entropy)
Concept drift — model decay as attacker behavior and legitimate traffic shift over time

sections.heading: Detection metrics
items: Precision — of all flagged alerts, how many were real
Recall — of all real attacks, how many were flagged
Threshold tuning — sliding the decision cutoff trades precision against recall
Alert fatigue — when false positives train analysts to ignore the queue
DGA — domain generation algorithm; detected via character entropy of domain names

sections.heading: Agent and LLM security
items: Direct prompt injection — attacker input overrides app instructions (OWASP LLM01:2025, the #1 LLM risk)
Indirect prompt injection — hidden instructions inside retrieved data (email, web, docs)
Jailbreak — defeating the model's own safety policy; distinct from hijacking app behavior
Tool poisoning — malicious tool descriptions or metadata steer an agent to misuse its tools (MCP ecosystem risk)
Insecure output handling — executing or trusting model output without validation
Least-privilege tools — grant each tool only the scope its task requires

sections.heading: Adversarial ML and governance
items: Evasion — perturbing inputs at inference time to dodge a classifier
Poisoning — corrupting training data to corrupt the model
Extraction — querying a model to steal its behavior or parameters
MITRE ATLAS — knowledge base of adversarial ML tactics and techniques
Red-teaming and evals — adversarial testing of AI systems before deployment
Human-in-the-loop — required approval for high-impact or irreversible agent actions
SOAR — security orchestration, automation and response; automate enrichment, gate containment

glossary.def: Default-deny execution control: only explicitly approved applications, scripts, and installers may run.
Default-allow model: everything runs except recognized-bad items — the window zero-days live in.
Deny-by-default posture: unknown code, devices, or connections are refused unless explicitly approved.
Containment applied on top of allowlisting; restricts what a permitted app may do across app-to-app, file, registry, and network dimensions.
Agent mode that catalogs applications and dependencies and auto-builds policies before enforcement; temporarily disables file blocking.
Temporary mode that pauses file blocking for installs — must be tightly scoped and time-boxed.
Grants specific approved applications admin rights for standard users — just-in-time, per-app, time-boxed — without standing admin rights.
An elevated or trusted process spawning another tool (e.g., PowerShell) to inherit its privileges — countered by ringfencing the elevated process.
Device and path policy: USB approved by serial, user, file type, time, and encryption; unapproved devices do not connect.
Centrally managed host firewall; rules by port, source IP, and dynamic ACLs; egress allowlisting pins apps to approved destinations.
Zero Trust Network Access: per-session, per-application brokered connections (commonly over port 443) with no open inbound ports — deny-by-default for network access.
Portal queue where end-user software requests arrive for admin review and decision.
Real-time audit showing what was allowed or denied across endpoints — and why; the evidence layer for triage.
One-button cloud VDI sandbox launched from an approval request; logs AV flags, canary-file access, and registry/system changes.
24/7/365 US-based managed detection and response team; validates alerts, isolates hosts, acts on customer runbooks; ~60-second average response.
Design and operate as if the attacker already has a foothold — least privilege, containment, and monitoring everywhere.
Attacks that hijack trusted built-in tools (Word, PowerShell) instead of dropping malware — defeated by behavior containment, not signatures.
Scoped, ticketed, tested changes with validation and rollback — emergency speed never cancels the process.
A node in an attack graph representing a system or weakness, connected by edges that represent steps an attacker could take between them.
How central a node is to paths through the graph (for example, betweenness: how many shortest paths cross it).
The most valuable assets in the environment (customer data, finance systems, source code): what attack paths are measured against.
A labeled connection between two nodes, representing a relationship such as 'logged into' or 'resolved to'.
A graph of threat indicators (IPs, domains, hashes) linked to campaigns, actors, and each other through shared infrastructure.
The practice of mapping relationships in data to reveal hidden associations; rooted in Euler's 1736 graph theory, 1970s paper link charts, and post-2001 intelligence work.
A segment of the network so small that its allowed communications can be enumerated as a graph of approved edges.
An entity in the graph: a user, host, IP address, domain, file, or vulnerability.
Access control where policy is evaluated by traversing relationships on a graph (for example: user reports_to manager who owns the resource's project).
A machine-learning model that operates directly on graph structure to classify nodes or subgraphs, for example labeling attack vs normal behavior.
Monitoring user and entity behavior by modeling their normal relationship patterns and flagging structural anomalies.
ML trained on labeled examples; classifies new inputs into known categories.
ML approach that models normal behavior and flags statistically rare deviations.
Turning raw telemetry into numeric model inputs, e.g. login velocity or domain entropy.
Share of flagged alerts that were real; the false-positive economics of the queue.
Share of real attacks the detector flagged; the miss rate's complement.
Decay of model performance as the data distribution shifts over time.
Attacker-crafted instructions that override an LLM application's intended behavior; direct (user input) or indirect (retrieved data).
Crafted input that defeats an LLM's own safety policy or refusal behavior.
Malicious tool descriptions or metadata that manipulate an AI agent into misusing its tools.
Failing to validate LLM output before acting on it, e.g. executing generated commands.
Adversarial ML technique: perturbing inputs to cross a classifier's decision boundary.
Adversarial Threat Landscape for AI Systems; MITRE's knowledge base of AI attack tactics.
Security orchestration, automation and response; playbooks that enrich automatically and gate containment on humans.
Required human approval before high-impact or irreversible automated actions.
